'''Donal Donat Conor Bradley''' is a British physicist who is the Vice President for Research at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology ([[Kaust|KAUST]]), Saudi Arabia. From 2015 until 2019, he was head of the [[Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences Division, University of Oxford|Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences Division]] of the [[University of Oxford]] and a Professor of Engineering Science and Physics at [[Jesus College, Oxford]]. From 2006 to 2015, he was the Lee-Lucas Professor of Experimental Physics at [[Imperial College London]]. He was the founding director of the Centre for Plastic Electronics<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www3.imperial.ac.uk/plasticelectronics|title=Centre for Plastic Electronics|date=8 March 2024 }}</ref> and served as vice-provost for research at the college.

Bradley is known for his contributions to the development of molecular electronic materials and devices.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold/faraday/medallists/page_38449.html|title=2009 Faraday Medal}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://conferences.theiet.org/achievement/senior/faraday.cfm|title=2010 Faraday Medal|access-date=1 March 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130108051729/http://conferences.theiet.org/achievement/senior/faraday.cfm|archive-date=8 January 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> Plastic or [[printed electronics]], as this technology is widely known, embodies a paradigm shift towards low temperature, solution-based device fabrication with applications in energy efficient displays and lighting, photovoltaic energy generation, medical diagnostics and longer term potential for optical communications.<ref name=gs>{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref name=friend/><ref name=nature1/><ref name=WadeSteiner2014>{{cite journal|last1=Wade|first1=Jessica|authorlink1=Jess Wade|last2=Steiner|first2=Florian|last3=Niedzialek|first3=Dorota|last4=James|first4=David T.|last5=Jung|first5=Youngsuk|last6=Yun|first6=Dong-Jin|last7=Bradley|first7=Donal D. C.|last8=Nelson|first8=Jenny|last9=Kim|first9=Ji-Seon|title=Charge mobility anisotropy of functionalized pentacenes in organic field effect transistors fabricated by solution processing|journal=Journal of Materials Chemistry C|volume=2|issue=47|year=2014|pages=10110–10115|issn=2050-7526|doi=10.1039/C4TC01353K}}</ref>

==Education==
Bradley was a pupil and latterly Head Boy at the Jesuit [[Wimbledon College]] in the [[London Borough of Merton]]. He studied as an undergraduate student (BSc Physics) at [[Imperial College London]] between 1980 and 1983 and obtained a first class honours degree and Associateship of the Royal College of Science. He was awarded the Royal Society for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce Silver Medal and fellowship ([[FRSA]]) as an outstanding graduate of the [[Royal College of Science]] and served in his second year as the Royal College of Science Union Departmental Representative for Physics. His postgraduate research was undertaken in the Physics and Chemistry of Solids Group at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]], [[University of Cambridge]], and he received a PhD in 1987.<ref name=PhDdd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/21857046?style=html|title=Spectroscopic investigations of the processible conjugated polymers poly(P-phenylene vinylene) and poly(4,4'-diphenylene diphenyl vinylene)|first= Donal D. C.|last=Bradley|date=1987|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.384283}}|website=jisc.ac.uk|oclc=|hdl=}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After completing his PhD in 1987 he was briefly a postdoctoral research associate funded by [[BP|British Petroleum]] before being simultaneously awarded the Unilever Research Fellowship in Chemical Physics at [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge]] (held 1987 – 1989), and a Toshiba Research Fellowship to work at the Toshiba Corporation Research and Development Center's Chemical Laboratory in Kawasaki, Japan (held 1987–88). {{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

Upon returning to [[Corpus Christi College, Cambridge]], after a year spent in Japan studying the nonlinear optical properties of poly(arylenevinylene) polymers, he played a central role in the February 1989 discovery of conjugated polymer electroluminescence, suggesting the experiment that led to [[Jeremy Burroughes|Jeremy Henley Burroughes']] first observation of light emission.<ref name=nature1>{{cite journal|last1=Burroughes|first1=J. H.|last2=Bradley|first2=D. D. C.|last3=Brown|first3=A. R.|last4=Marks|first4=R. N.|last5=Mackay|first5=K.|last6=Friend|first6=R. H.|last7=Burns|first7=P. L.|last8=Holmes|first8=A. B.|title=Light-emitting diodes based on conjugated polymers|journal=Nature|volume=347|issue=6293|year=1990|pages=539–541|issn=0028-0836|doi=10.1038/347539a0|bibcode=1990Natur.347..539B|s2cid=43158308}}</ref>  Together with Jeremy Burroughes he undertook the initial characterisation of the basic properties of [[Poly(p-phenylene vinylene)|poly(p-phenylenevinylene)]] [[organic light emitting diode|light emitting diodes]], demonstrating that the light emission phenomenon was injection electroluminescence and that the frequency response was sufficiently fast to permit video display applications. Recognizing the importance of their discovery Bradley and Burroughes decided that it should be patented and together with [[Richard Friend]]<ref name=friend>{{cite journal|last1=Friend|first1=R. H.|last2=Gymer|first2=R. W.|last3=Holmes|first3=A. B.|last4=Burroughes|first4=J. H.|last5=Marks|first5=R. N.|last6=Taliani|first6=C.|last7=Bradley|first7=D. D. C.|last8=Santos|first8=D. A. Dos|last9=Brédas|first9=J. L.|last10=Lögdlund|first10=M.|last11=Salaneck|first11=W. R.|author9-link=Jean-Luc Brédas|title=Electroluminescence in conjugated polymers|journal=Nature|volume=397|issue=6715|year=1999|pages=121–128|issn=0028-0836|doi=10.1038/16393|bibcode=1999Natur.397..121F|s2cid=4328634}}</ref> filed a GB patent (PCT/GB90.00584)<ref>{{cite web|title=Electroluminescent devices|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/CA2030785C/pt|publisher=Google Patents|access-date=2016-06-13|date=20 April 1989}}</ref> with first claim:<blockquote>''An electroluminescent device comprising a semiconductor layer in the form of a thin dense polymer film comprising at least one conjugated polymer;''<br>''a first contact layer which is selected so that on application of an electric field to said device charge carriers of a first type are injected into the semiconductor layer;'' ''and a second contact layer which is selected so that on application of an electric field to said device charge carriers of a second type are injected into the semiconductor layers, wherein the polymer film of the semiconductor layer has sufficiently low concentration of extrinsic charge carriers that on applying an electric field between the first and second contact layers across the semiconductor layer as to render the second contact layer positive relative to the first contact layer charge carriers of said first and second types are injected into the semiconductor layer and combine to form in the conjugated polymer charge carrier pairs which decay radiatively so that radiation is emitted from the conjugated polymer.''</blockquote>

Bradley was the corresponding author for the subsequent 1990 ''Nature'' paper reporting the discovery of conjugated polymer electroluminescence.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Nature|volume=347|issue=6293|pages=539–541|doi=10.1038/347539a0|year=1990|url=http://www.nature.com/physics/looking-back/burroughes/index.html|title=Light-emitting diodes based on conjugated polymers|last1=Burroughes|first1=J. H.|last2=Bradley|first2=D. D. C.|last3=Brown|first3=A. R.|last4=Marks|first4=R. N.|last5=MacKay|first5=K.|last6=Friend|first6=R. H.|last7=Burns|first7=P. L.|last8=Holmes|first8=A. B.|bibcode=1990Natur.347..539B|s2cid=43158308|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This paper rapidly became the most highly cited paper in the field of molecular electronic materials and devices – a position that it holds to this day – and it triggered an explosion of activity around the world, thereby launching the new field of plastic electronics.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.epsrc.ac.uk/newsevents/pubs/the-economic-benefits-of-chemistry-research-to-the-uk/|title=The Economic Benefit of Chemistry Research to the UK|page=113|date=September 2010|publisher=Oxford Economics}}</ref>

Bradley is an [[Institute for Scientific Information]] highly cited author<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hcr3.isiknowledge.com/author.cgi?&link1=Search&link2=Search%20Results&AuthLastName=bradley&AuthFirstName=&AuthMiddleName=&AuthMailnstName=&CountryID=-1&DisciplineID=0&id=1987|title=ISI Highly Cited, Donal Bradley|accessdate=2014-09-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070519223724/http://hcr3.isiknowledge.com/author.cgi|archive-date=19 May 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref> in both Materials Science and Physics with 563 papers published to date. His [[h-index]] in January 2019 is 109 and his publications have been cited a combined total of 59,482 times (ISI Web of Science). {{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

Bradley joined the [[University of Oxford]] in 2015<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www2.physics.ox.ac.uk/contacts/people/bradley|title=Donal Bradley {{!}} University of Oxford Department of Physics|website=www2.physics.ox.ac.uk|language=en|access-date=2018-08-17}}</ref> as Head of the Mathematical, Physical and Life Sciences Division and Professor of Physics and [[Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford|Engineering Science]]. He is a Professorial Fellow of Jesus College.

Bradley was one of the 21 members of Oxford congress who stood to oppose the debate on the university's response to a changes proposed to the [[Universities Superannuation Scheme]] (USS) in March 2018.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2018/mar/06/oxford-university-blocks-challenge-to-staff-pension-cuts-proposals-universities-strike|title=Opposition to Oxford USS Debate.|website=[[TheGuardian.com]] |date=6 March 2018 |last1=Adams |first1=Richard }}</ref><ref>{{Cite tweet |user=sallylepage |number=971309984712716294 |date = 7 March 2018 |title=Bradley Opposition }}</ref>

On 7 April 2019 Bradley joined King Abdullah University of Science and Technology ([[Kaust|KAUST]]) as the Vice President for Research.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Donal D. C. Bradley|url=https://www.kaust.edu.sa/en/study/faculty/donal-d-c-bradley|access-date=2021-04-25|website=www.kaust.edu.sa}}</ref>

==Awards and prizes==
Bradley's research has been recognised by:
{{div col|colwidth=35em}}
*the Founders Prize of the combined Institute of Physics, Royal Society of Chemistry and Institute of Materials, Minerals and Mining, Polymer Physics Group (2013)
*the [[Institution of Engineering and Technology]] [[Faraday Medal]] (2010),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theiet.org/about/media-centre/press-releases/20100419.cfm|title=Institution of Engineering and Technology Faraday Medal 2010|accessdate=2014-09-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110225214510/http://www.theiet.org/about/media-centre/press-releases/20100419.cfm|archive-date=25 February 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*the [[Institute of Physics]] [[Faraday Medal and Prize|Faraday Medal]] (2009),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold/faraday/medallists/page_38449.html|title=Institute of Physics Faraday Medal 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://nispconnect.wordpress.com/2009/08/11/application-of-physics|title=Norman's Blog|date=11 August 2009 |accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>

*the [[Imperial College London]] Research Excellence Award (2006),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://acrongen.com/filesmain/Research%20Excellence%20for%20MV%20From%20Imperial.pdf|title=Imperial College London Research Excellence Award 2006|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>
*the [[European Science Foundation]] European Latsis Prize for Nanoengineering (2005),<ref>{{Cite FTP |url=ftp://ftp.cordis.europa.eu/pub/ist/docs/dir_g/newsletter_115.pdf|server=FTP server|url-status=dead|title=European Science Foundation European Latsis Prize 2005|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>
*the [[Society for Information Display]] Jan Rajchman Prize (2005),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.opera2015.org/newsletters/EPIC_NEWS_VOL2/epicv2n1_version_finale.pdf|title=Quarterly Epic Newsletter for Photonics|accessdate=2014-09-06}}{{Dead link|date=November 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sid.org/conf/sid2005/program/advprog.pdf|title=SID 2005 Programme|accessdate=2014-09-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080705205841/http://www.sid.org/conf/sid2005/program/advprog.pdf|archive-date=5 July 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imperial.ac.uk/college.asp?P=6952|title=Imperial College Jan Rajchman Prize Announcement|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>
*the European Union [[Descartes Prize]] (2003) for ''"Polymer Light-Emitting Diodes for displays (PLEDD)"''
*and a [[Daiwa Adrian Prize|Daiwa Award]] (1994).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dajf.org.uk/_pdf/DAP%202010%20fact%20sheet.pdf|title=Daiwa Award 1994|accessdate=2014-09-06}}{{Dead link|date=November 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
{{div col end}}
He was also the recipient of the Royal Society for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce Silver Medal in 1983 as an outstanding graduate of the Royal College of Science. He was elected a fellow of the Royal Society for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce ([[FRSA]]) in 1983, a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2004,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imperial.ac.uk/college.asp?P=5260|title=FRS Imperial College Announcement 2004}}</ref> a fellow of the Institute of Physics (FInstP) in 2005 and a fellow of the Institution of Engineering and Technology (FIET) in 2013.

In the [[2010 New Year Honours#Commanders of the Order of the British Empire .28CBE.29|New Year Honours 2010]] Bradley was appointed as a [[Commander of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) by the Queen for ''services to science''.<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=59282|date=31 December 2009|page=6|supp=y}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/honours-list-order-of-the-british-empire-cbe-1853550.html|title=CBE Announcement Independent|location=London, UK|work=The Independent|date=31 December 2009|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/8435305.stm|title=CBE Announcement BBC|publisher=BBC News|first=Jason|last=Palmer|date=31 December 2009|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/news/jan10/page_42473.html|title=CBE Announcement IoP|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>

===Named lectures===
Bradley delivered the first Nanjing Tech Global Vision Lecture (annual distinguished lecture) on "Molecular Control for Plastic Electronics and Photonics" in July 2013. {{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

In February 2011 he delivered the Distinguished Lecture in Physics on "Molecular Control for Conjugated Polymer Optics and Photonics" at [[Hong Kong Baptist University]]. {{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

in March 2010, he delivered the [[Bakerian Lecture|Royal Society Bakerian Lecture]] on "Plastic Electronics: their science and applications”.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/Bakerian-Lecture-2010|title=The Royal Society Bakerian Lecture 2010|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>

In December 2009 he delivered the [[Institute of Physics]] Mott Lecture on ''"Plastic Electronics – The Science and Application of Molecular Electronic Materials and Devices" ''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.soton.ac.uk/~fangohr/software/ovf2vtk/news/CMMP2009_Announcement.pdf|title=The Institute of Physics Mott Lecture 2009|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>

In November of the same year he delivered the [[Hong Kong Polytechnic University]] Chau Wai-yin Memorial Lecture ''"Twenty Years of Plastic Electronics – The Science and Application of Molecular Electronic Materials"''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.polyu.edu.hk/iao/cwy|title=Hong Kong Polytechnic University Chau-wai Yin Memorial Lecture 2009|access-date=1 March 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721090810/http://www.polyu.edu.hk/iao/cwy/|archive-date=21 July 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> and in October the [[University of Liverpool]] Frolich Lecture ''"The Science and Application of Molecular Electronic Materials and Devices"''. {{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

In 2005 Bradley delivered the European Science Foundation European Latsis Prize Lecture ''"Nano-Engineering a Molecular Electronic Future"'' at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, France, the [[Institute of Physics]] Ireland Lecture Series (at [[Trinity College, Dublin]], [[University College Cork]] and [[National University of Ireland, Galway|University College Galway]]) ''"Organic Electronics: A Molecular Vision”'' and in 2004 the Weissberger-Williams Lecture (same title) at the [[Eastman Kodak]] Company's R&D Laboratories in [[Rochester, New York]] (USA).

===Other honours===
Bradley has been ranked since 2002 by the Institute for Scientific Information as one of the 1% most highly cited physicists in the world for research published over the past two decades.<ref name="EyeSight">[http://www.isihighlycited.com Highly Cited, Rankings by Citation]</ref> Additionally he has been ranked since 2010 as one of the 1% most highly cited materials scientists in the world for research published over the past two decades.<ref name="EyeSight"/>

He is also ranked by the Institute for Scientific Information as one of the top 100 materials scientists in the world on the basis of the impact (citations per paper) of his journal papers published between 2000 and 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/Journals/THE/THE/24_February_2011/attachments/Top%20Materials%20Scientists.pdf|title=THE list of top 100 material scientists 2000–2010|accessdate=2014-09-06}}</ref>
